solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Was keeping Republican popular a dangerous thing in the main? (7)

definitions.text: a dangerous thing in the main

indicators.note: WAS keeps R held inside it

annotation.surface: A question about whether backing a popular Republican was a dangerous move in the main race or contest.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The main' is the old poetic word for the open sea, so the definition is a cryptic description of a fighting ship, not a political risk.
annotation.definitionFit: A warship is a dangerous thing to meet on the high seas, the main.

entries.clue: Pork pie with insect underneath (7)

indicators.note: in a down entry the second piece is written underneath the first, so HOPPER goes below W

blocks.note: a hopper is a leaping insect such as a grasshopper

annotation.surface: A pork pie with a bug found lurking underneath it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pork pie' is Cockney rhyming slang for a lie (porky pie), and a whopper is a big lie. 'Underneath' places HOPPER below W in this down entry.
annotation.definitionFit: A whopper is a blatant lie, which rhyming slang calls a pork pie.

entries.clue: Fix section of armrest – or else! (7)

indicators.note: the answer is a section cut from the run of letters that follows

annotation.surface: A menacing order to repair the broken part of a chair's armrest, or face the consequences.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash and 'or else!' make it read as a threat, which hides the word straddling three words.
annotation.definitionFit: To restore something is to fix it back to its former condition.

entries.clue: Building hotel next to river (5)

blocks.note: H is Hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the Ouse is a river in England

annotation.surface: An estate agent's line about a building beside a hotel on the riverside.
annotation.walkthrough: The Ouse is one of several English rivers of that name, a setter's favourite.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym by example: a home is the everyday kind of building the word names.

entries.clue: Pert bust initially trembling under items of clothing – most fetching (9)

indicators.note: bust = broken, so PERT is broken up
take the first letter of trembling
in a down entry, T sits under TIES

annotation.surface: A racy lingerie-catalogue line about a trembling bust beneath garments.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bust' looks like a body part in this surface but is the anagram instruction, meaning broken.
annotation.definitionFit: Fetching is an old-fashioned word for attractive, so the superlative matches a superlative of good-looking.

entries.clue: Harry ultimately drives black and white diggers (7)

indicators.note: take the final letter of drives

blocks.note: to harry someone is to badger them

annotation.surface: Prince Harry, in the end, drives some black-and-white vehicles or animals.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Harry' reads as a name but is the verb meaning to pester.
annotation.definitionFit: Badgers are black-and-white striped animals that dig setts.

entries.clue: Located a shilling in the sack (5)

indicators.note: 'in the sack' places what comes before it inside the sack, so A and S sit within BED

blocks.note: the sack is slang for bed
S is the abbreviation for a shilling, an old British coin

annotation.surface: Someone found a shilling lying in a sack.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The sack' is slang for bed, as in 'hit the sack'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an office located in London has its headquarters, its base, there.

entries.clue: Leaving reader put out (9)

indicators.note: 'out' as in a bone out of joint: the letters are knocked from their places

annotation.surface: A reader, put out, walks off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Put out' reads as a phrase meaning annoyed, but 'put' is fodder and only 'out' is the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Read as a noun, 'leaving' is the act of going away, as in 'his leaving was sudden'.

entries.clue: Stylish European on stage with a set of books (7)

indicators.note: in a down entry, one thing on another sits above it, so E is placed on top of LEG

blocks.note: a leg is a stage of a journey or race
NT = New Testament, a set of books of the Bible

annotation.surface: A chic European performer on stage holding a stack of books.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stage' suggests a theatre but means a leg of a journey; the set of books is the New Testament.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: graceful and refined in appearance or manner, as a well-cut suit is.

entries.clue: Use bad language about bounds of triple jumper (7)

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so SWEAR is wrapped around TE
the bounds of a word are its first and last letters

blocks.note: to swear is to use bad language
first and last letters of triple

annotation.surface: An athlete curses the limits of the triple jump.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Triple jumper' looks like an athlete, but the phrase splits: 'triple' supplies letters and 'jumper', the British word for a sweater, is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: In British English a jumper is a knitted sweater.

entries.clue: Confuse old boy with second course of treatment (7)

blocks.note: OB = old boy, a former pupil
a cure is a course of treatment

annotation.surface: An elderly man is bewildered by a second round of medical treatment.
annotation.walkthrough: OB, old boy, is a former pupil of a British school.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to muddy an issue so that nobody can see it clearly.

entries.clue: Most excellent drink – remember? Not half! (7)

indicators.note: only half of remember is used

annotation.surface: A boozy exchange: an excellent drink, remember it? Not half!
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'absolutely', which disguises the instruction to use only half a word.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: highest in quality or rank, as in a supreme court or effort.

entries.clue: In favour of exam? Edward expressed opposition (9)

annotation.surface: Asked whether he backed the exam, Edward objected.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark splits the clue into a dialogue, but the parts simply run on in order.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense: objected, spoke out against something.

entries.clue: Cook in oven or pan (5)

blocks.note: dry-heat cooking of meat or vegetables in an oven
to pan a play is to criticise it harshly

annotation.surface: A recipe choice: cook it in the oven or in a pan.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pan' reads as a cooking pot but is the verb for savaging a review, so the kitchen picture hides a second meaning.
annotation.definitionFit: Critics who pan a show roast it; cooks roast meat in the oven.

entries.clue: Tries displacing river birds (5)

indicators.note: the R, river, of HEARS is moved to the front

blocks.note: a judge hears or tries a case

annotation.surface: Someone attempts to move some water birds off a river.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tries' is legal: a court tries a case, that is, hears it. Moving its R (river) to the front gives the birds.
annotation.definitionFit: Rheas are large flightless South American birds.

entries.clue: Frightening bird protecting rear of nest (9)

indicators.note: STARLING protects T by surrounding it
the rear of a word is its back end, so only the final letter of nest is taken

annotation.surface: A scary bird guarding the back of its nest.
annotation.walkthrough: The bird is not frightening; 'Frightening' is the definition and the bird is a starling.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: giving a sudden shock or fright.

entries.clue: Parisian in bar fight (9)

blocks.note: a counter is a bar where drinks are served

annotation.surface: A Frenchman gets into a brawl in a bar.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container instruction but it is the word a Parisian would say: EN.
annotation.definitionFit: An encounter can be a clash or fight between enemies.

entries.clue: Things chaps once put on fish slices (9)

annotation.surface: Men used to put slices of fish on something.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Put on' reads as placing food on a plate but means wearing: a codpiece was a pouch worn over the groin in Tudor times.
annotation.definitionFit: Codpieces were garments men once wore over their breeches.

entries.clue: Pulled in cart at ground with Ted (9)

indicators.note: ground = crushed, so CART AT is ground up

annotation.surface: Ted was pulled into a cart at a sports ground.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like a place but is the anagram instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: To attract a crowd is to pull it in.

entries.clue: Almost everyone bearing weapons is agitated (7)

indicators.note: ALL loses its last letter

annotation.surface: Nearly everyone carrying guns is jumpy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Almost' trims one letter from the end of ALL; the surface reads straight, which is why it is easy to miss that 'is' is only a link.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: worried and flustered, as someone who has had a fright is.

entries.clue: Little time before French composer’s journeys (7)

indicators.note: 'before' means ahead of, so the time letter is placed ahead of the composer

blocks.note: T = time, and a single letter is little
Maurice Ravel was a French composer

annotation.surface: A French composer's trips, just before his time ran short.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s of 'composer’s' is kept as a letter S; Ravel wrote Boléro.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as a plural noun: trips abroad, as in Gulliver's.

entries.clue: Ecstasy as golfer oddly gets score of two under par (5)

indicators.note: take the odd-numbered letters of 'as golfer'

blocks.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy
A s G o L f E r

annotation.surface: A golfer on drugs plays erratically yet cards a two under par.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' looks like it describes the golfer's play, but it picks letters from both 'as' and 'golfer'.
annotation.definitionFit: In golf an eagle is a hole played two strokes under par.

entries.clue: Rubbish clothing wise man first ignored (7)

indicators.note: SAGE with its first letter ignored

annotation.surface: A scruffy wise man's clothes are dismissed as rubbish.
annotation.walkthrough: 'First ignored' reads as the sage being snubbed, but it drops the S at the front of SAGE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, the American word for household waste, and also used for nonsense.

entries.clue: Non-stop lewdness aroused no wife (7)

indicators.note: 'aroused' means stirred up, and stirred letters change places
'no wife' means without the wife, so the W is taken away

blocks.note: W = wife, taken out of LEWDNESS

annotation.surface: Constant smut stirred up, but not the wife.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Aroused' fits the lewd surface but is the stirring instruction for the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: going on without a break, as endless chatter does.

entries.clue: A piece is cut off (5)

blocks.note: a portion or component of a whole

annotation.surface: A slice has been severed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A piece' looks like the subject of the sentence, but it is simply the letters of the answer split in two.
annotation.definitionFit: Something apart is separated, cut off from the rest.

entries.clue: Quietly muttered we’d perish at sea (9)

indicators.note: at sea = confused, all over the place

annotation.surface: A sailor murmurs that they would die out on the ocean.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At sea' completes a gloomy sailor's line, but means muddled.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: spoke under the breath, so softly that only someone close could hear.

entries.clue: Stitch up involving a good salary (5)

indicators.note: in a down entry, up turns SEW round
to involve is to take in, so the reversed stitch takes A and G inside it

annotation.surface: A framing scheme involving someone's well-paid job.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stitch up' reads as the British phrase for framing someone, but it splits into stitch (SEW) and up (reverse).
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: regular pay received for work.

entries.clue: Pokes one’s nose in cup, by the sound of it (5)

indicators.note: we hear the word rather than read it

annotation.surface: Someone sticks their nose into a teacup, apparently.
annotation.walkthrough: The cup is a trophy, not a teacup.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone who pries pokes their nose into others' business.

entries.clue: Observing this writer, for example, pinching money (7)

indicators.note: EG pinches TIN, holding it inside

blocks.note: tin is old British slang for money

annotation.surface: A writer is seen stealing some cash.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pinching' reads as stealing money, but it is EG holding TIN.
annotation.definitionFit: Meeting someone is seeing, observing them face to face.

entries.clue: Starts to cry loudly, improving friend’s mood (7)

indicators.note: the starts, first letters, of the three words

blocks.note: first letters of cry, loudly, improving
mate = friend; the 's joins as 'is', dropped

annotation.surface: Crying loudly makes a friend feel better.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Starts to cry' looks like someone beginning to weep but takes the first letter of three words.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: the prevailing atmosphere or feeling, as in 'the political climate'.

entries.clue: Editor turns and notices plans (7)

indicators.note: something that turns faces the other way, so the editor's letters run backwards

annotation.surface: A newspaper editor turns round and spots the schemes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Notices' reads as a verb, spots, but is the noun: posted signs.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as a plural noun: drawings or schemes made before building something.

entries.clue: Secret agent, with no pressure, checks arrangements (7)

indicators.note: 'with no pressure' means lacking the P that stands for pressure, so it is removed

blocks.note: to stem a flow is to check it

annotation.surface: A relaxed spy inspects the setup.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Checks' reads as inspects, but it means halts, as in stemming a flow.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: organised set-ups, as in a filing or seating arrangement.
